source_text: Sunt plane et alia tam stulta, quae pertinent ad contumelias et passiones Dei; aut prudentiam dicant Deum crucifixum. Aufer hoc quoque, Marcion, imo hoc potius. Quid enim indignius Deo? quid magis erubescendum, nasci an mori? carnem gestare, an crucem? circumcidi, an suffigi? educari, an sepeliri? in praesepe deponi, an in monumento recondi? Sapientior eris, si nec ista credideris. Sed non eris sapiens, nisi stultus saeculo fueris, Dei stulta credendo. An ideo passiones a Christo non rescidisti, quia ut phantasma vacabat a sensu earum? Diximus retro aeque illum et nativitatis et infantiae imaginariae vacua ludibria subire potuisse. Sed jam hic responde, interfector veritatis. Nonne vere crucifixus est Deus? nonne vere mortuus, ut vere crucifixus? nonne vere resuscitatus, ut vere scilicet mortuus? Falso ergo statuit inter nos scire Paulus tantum Jesum crucifixum? falso sepulturum ingessit? falso resuscitatum inculcavit? Falsa est igitur et fides nostra, et phantasma est totum quod speramus a Christo? Scelestissime hominum, qui interemptores excusas Dei. Nihil enim ab eis passus est Christus, si nihil vere est passus. Parce unicae spei totius orbis. Quid destruis necessarium dedecus fidei? Quodcumque Deo indignum est, mihi expedit. Salvus sum, si non confundar de Domino meo. Qui mei, inquit, confusus fuerit, confundar et ego ejus. Alias non invenio materias confusionis, quae me per contemptum ruboris probent bene impudentem et feliciter stultum. Natus est Dei Filius; non pudet, quia pudendum est: et mortuus est Dei Filius; prorsus credibile est, quia ineptum est: et sepultus, resurrexit; certum est, quia impossibile. Sed haec quomodo in illo vera erunt, si ipse non fuit verus, si non vere habuit in se quod figeretur, quod moreretur, quod sepeliretur et resuscitaretur, carnem scilicet sanguine suffusam, ossibus structam, nervis intextam, venis implexam, quae nasci et mori novit? Humana sine dubio, ut nata de homine; ideoque mortalis haec erit in Christo, quia Christus homo et filius hominis. Aut cur homo Christus et filius hominis, si nihil hominis et nihil ex homine? nisi si aut aliud est homo quam caro, aut aliunde caro hominis, quam ex homine; aut aliud Maria, quam homo, aut homo deus Marcionis. Aliter, non diceretur homo Christus, sine carne; nec hominis filius, sine aliquo parente homine: sicut nec Deus, sine Spiritu Dei; nec Dei Filius, sine Deo patre. ita utriusque substantiae census hominem et Deum exhibuit: hinc natum, inde non natum; hinc carneum, inde spiritalem; hinc infirmum, inde praefortem; hinc morientem, inde viventem. Quae proprietas conditionum, divinae et humanae, aequa utique naturae utriusque veritate dispuncta est, eadem fide, et spiritus et carnis. Virtutes spiritum Dei, passiones carnem hominis probaverunt. Si virtutes non sine spiritu, proinde et passiones non sine carne: si caro cum passionibus ficta, et spiritus ergo cum virtutibus falsus. Quid dimidias mendacio Christum? Totus veritas fuit. Maluit, crede, nasci, quam ex aliqua parte mentiri, et quidem in semetipsum; ut carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram, sine musculis solidam, sine sanguine cruentam, sine tunica vestitam, sine fame esurientem, sine dentibus edentem, sine lingua loquentem; ut phantasma auribus fuerit sermo ejus per imaginem vocis. Fuit itaque phantasma etiam post resurrectionem, cum manus et pedes suos discipulis inspiciendos offerret: Aspicite, inquit, quod ego sum, quia spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me habentem videtis, sine dubio manus et pedes et ossa, quae spiritus non habet, sed caro. Quomodo hanc vocem interpretaris, Marcion, qui a Deo optimo, et simplici, et bono tantum, infers Jesum? Ecce fallit et decipit, et circumvenit omnium oculos, omnium sensus, omnium accessus et contractus. Ergo jam Christum non de coelo deferre debueras, sed de aliquo circulatorio coetu; nec Deum praeter hominem, sed magum hominem; nec salutis pontificem, sed spectaculi artificem; nec mortuorum suscitatorem, sed vivorum avocatorem. Nisi quod et si magus fuit, natus est.
pass_a_gloss: There are also other foolish things that pertain to the insults and passions of God; or they say that God was crucified prudently. Take away also this, Marcion, or rather take away this especially. For what is more unworthy of God? What is more to be blushed at, to be born or to die? To carry flesh or to carry a cross? To be circumcised or to be nailed? To be brought up or to be buried? To be laid in a manger or to be hidden in a tomb? You will be wiser if you do not believe these things. But you will not be wise unless you have been foolish in the eyes of the world, believing the foolish things of God. Or is it for this reason that you did not cut off the passions from Christ, because as a phantom he was free from the sense of them? We said earlier that he was equally able to undergo the imaginary mockeries of birth and infancy. But now respond, you killer of truth. Was God not truly crucified? Was God not truly dead, so that he was truly crucified? Was God not truly resurrected, so that he was truly dead? Therefore, does Paul falsely establish that he knows Jesus as crucified? Does he falsely introduce his burial? Does he falsely inculcate his resurrection? Therefore, our faith is false, and everything we hope for from Christ is a phantom? You are the most wicked of men, who excuse the killers of God. For Christ did not suffer anything from them if he did not truly suffer. Spare the only hope of the whole world. Why do you destroy the necessary shame of faith? Whatever is unworthy of God is expedient for me. I am saved if I am not ashamed of my Lord. He who is ashamed of me, I will be ashamed of him. I do not find other materials of shame that prove me to be well shameless and happily foolish through contempt of shame. The Son of God was born; I am not ashamed, because it is shameful: and the Son of God died; it is entirely believable because it is foolish: and he was buried and rose again; it is certain because it is impossible. But how will these things be true in him if he himself was not true, if he did not truly have in himself what was fixed, what died, what was buried and rose again, namely flesh suffused with blood, structured with bones, intertwined with nerves, and entwined with veins, which knows how to be born and die? It is certainly human, as born from a human; and therefore this will be mortal in Christ, because Christ is human and the son of a human. Or why is Christ human and the son of a human, if he is nothing of a human and nothing from a human? Unless perhaps a human is something other than flesh, or human flesh is from somewhere other than a human; or perhaps Mary is something other than a human, or a human is the god of Marcion. Otherwise, Christ would not be called human without flesh; nor would he be called the son of a human without some human parent: just as God is not without the Spirit of God; nor is the Son of God without God the Father. So the census of both substances showed him to be human and God: born from one, not born from the other; fleshly from one, spiritual from the other; weak from one, very strong from the other; dying from one, living from the other. The property of divine and human conditions, equally true to the nature of both, is distinguished by the same faith, and by the spirit and the flesh. The virtues proved the Spirit of God, the passions proved the flesh of a human. If virtues are not without spirit, then passions are not without flesh: if flesh with passions is fictional, then spirit with virtues is false. Why do you make Christ half a lie? He was entirely truth. He preferred, believe me, to be born rather than to lie in any part, and indeed in himself; so that he might carry flesh without bones, hard without muscles, solid without blood, clothed without a tunic, hungry without food, eating without teeth, speaking without a tongue; so that his speech might be a phantom to the ears through the image of a voice. Therefore, he was also a phantom after the resurrection, when he offered his hands and feet to the disciples to be inspected: 'Behold', he says, 'what I am, because a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having, without a doubt hands and feet and bones, which a spirit does not have, but flesh.' How do you interpret this voice, Marcion, who infers Jesus from a good, simple, and optimal God? Behold, he deceives and cheats, and circumvents the eyes, senses, approaches, and contracts of all. Therefore, you ought not to have brought Christ down from heaven, but from some circus troupe; nor God besides a human, but a human magician; nor the pontiff of salvation, but the artisan of a spectacle; nor the raiser of the dead, but the caller of the living. Unless perhaps even if he was a magician, he was born.

pass_b_english: There are other foolish claims, too, that touch on the insults and sufferings of God—claims that call it prudent for God to have been crucified. Take that one back as well, Marcion; better yet, take it back first of all. What could be more unworthy of God? What is more shameful—to be born or to die? To bear flesh or to bear a cross? To be circumcised or to be nailed up? To be raised or to be buried? To be laid in a manger or hidden in a tomb? You would be wiser if you refused to believe such things. But you will never be wise unless you have become a fool in the world's eyes by believing the foolishness of God. Is that why you stripped the passions from Christ—because as a phantom he was exempt from feeling them? We have already shown he could just as well have undergone the imaginary mockeries of birth and infancy. But now answer me, you killer of truth. Was God not truly crucified? Was he not truly dead, so that he was truly crucified? Was he not truly raised, so that he was truly dead? Does Paul therefore falsely declare that he knows nothing but Jesus Christ and him crucified? Does he falsely hand down his burial? Does he falsely drill his resurrection into us? Is our faith therefore a lie, and everything we hope for from Christ a mere phantom? You are the most wicked of men, excusing the murderers of God. For Christ suffered nothing at their hands if he did not truly suffer. Spare the world's only hope. Why destroy the necessary shame of faith? Whatever is unworthy of God works for my salvation. I am saved if I am not ashamed of my Lord. 'Whoever is ashamed of me,' he says, 'I will be ashamed of him' (Mark 8:38). I find no other grounds for shame that would prove me gloriously shameless and happily foolish through contempt for shame. The Son of God was born; I am not ashamed, because it is shameful. The Son of God died; it is entirely believable because it is absurd. He was buried and rose again; it is certain because it is impossible. But how can these things be true in him if he himself was not true, if he did not truly possess in himself what could be pierced, what could die, what could be buried and raised—flesh suffused with blood, structured with bones, woven with nerves, laced with veins, flesh that knows how to be born and how to die? It is unquestionably human, since it was born of a human; and therefore this flesh is mortal in Christ, because Christ is human and the son of a human. Or why call Christ human and the son of a human if he shares nothing of humanity and derives nothing from a human? Unless a human is something other than flesh, or human flesh comes from somewhere other than a human; or Mary is something other than human, or the human is Marcion's god. Otherwise Christ would not be called human without flesh, nor the son of a human without a human parent—just as there is no God without the Spirit of God, and no Son of God without God the Father. So the inventory of both substances displayed him as both human and God: born from one side, unbegotten from the other; fleshly from one, spiritual from the other; weak from one, supremely strong from the other; dying from one, living from the other. The distinctive property of the two conditions, divine and human, each equally true to its own nature, is marked off by the same faith—by spirit and by flesh. The miracles proved the Spirit of God; the sufferings proved the flesh of a human. If miracles are not without spirit, then sufferings are not without flesh: if flesh with its sufferings is a fiction, then spirit with its miracles is a lie. Why make Christ half a lie? He was entirely truth. He chose, believe me, to be born rather than to falsify himself in any part—so that he might carry flesh without bones to harden it, without muscles to strengthen it, without blood to redden it, without skin to clothe it, hunger without food, eating without teeth, speaking without a tongue; so that his speech would be a phantom to the ear, a mere image of a voice. He was therefore a phantom even after the resurrection, when he offered his hands and feet for the disciples to inspect: 'Look at my hands and my feet; it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see I have' (Luke 24:39). How do you read that voice, Marcion, you who derive Jesus from a God who is only good, simple, and kind? Look: he deceives, he cheats, he evades every eye, every sense, every approach, every contact. You should not have brought Christ down from heaven, but from some circus troupe; not God beyond a human, but a human magician; not the high priest of salvation, but the stage-manager of a spectacle; not the raiser of the dead, but the caller-away of the living. Unless, of course, even a magician had to be born.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required scripture citations (Mark 8:38 and Luke 24:39) for the quoted/alluded passages. The translation of 'virtutes' as 'miracles' in the context of the Spirit's work is a valid theological rendering of the Latin, and 'census' as 'inventory' preserves the sense of a detailed account or listing of attributes. All clauses in the Latin are accounted for in both Pass A and B.

The Latin text is correctly identified as 'On the Flesh of Christ 5' from the specified edition. The translation accurately reflects the source text, with appropriate inline citations for biblical references. The title 'The Reality of Christ's Flesh' appropriately captures the content of the passage. No OCR damage or uncertain readings are noted in the supplied text.
